articles.title: Musk plans Cybertruck production wind-down by mid-2027 as Tesla shifts to Cybercab
articles.description: New Delhi: Elon Musk has announced plans to gradually wind down production of Tesla's Cybertruck at its Gigafactory in Texas by mid-2027 to make room for increased Cybercab manufacturing, marking a significant shift in the electric vehicle maker's strategy as it places greater emphasis on autonomous transportation. In a post on X, Musk said, "Tesla will be winding down production of the Cybertruck at Gigafactory Texas around the middle of next year to make room for increased Cybercab production." The proposed move comes just as Tesla has sharply increased Cybertruck prices in the United States and reportedly paused new orders for its most affordable Dual-Motor All-Wheel Drive variant. The developments raise questions about the future of a vehicle that Musk once projected could become one of Tesla's biggest commercial successes but which has struggled to achieve the anticipated sales volumes. Cybertruck gets costlier even as production wind-down looms Tesla's latest US pricing changes have made Cybertruck significantly more expensive, despite the company's plans to reduce its manufacturing footprint. The Cybertruck Premium AWD now starts at $92,490, compared with $84,990 earlier, representing an increase of $7,500, or approximately 8.8 per cent. The range-topping Cyberbeast has become 2.5 per cent more expensive, with its starting price rising from $99,990 to $102,490. Meanwhile, the entry-level Dual-Motor AWD variant, previously priced at $74,990, is now listed at $82,490, a 10 per cent increase. However, the configuration has reportedly been greyed out on Tesla's ordering platform, temporarily preventing customers from placing new orders. These increases follow another round of revisions in August 2026, when Tesla raised prices for the Dual-Motor AWD and Premium AWD models by $5,000 each. The Premium AWD, which started 2026 at $79,990, now costs $92,490, an increase of $12,500, or nearly 16 per cent. The entry-level Cybertruck has experienced an even sharper increase. Introduced in February at a promotional price of $59,990, the Dual-Motor AWD variant has become $22,500 more expensive at its latest listed price, a jump of approximately 37.5 per cent. The combination of higher prices and restricted availability suggests Tesla could be shifting Cybertruck towards a lower-volume, higher-priced segment rather than pursuing aggressive mass-market expansion. Higher prices could also help protect profit margins as production volumes decline, although Tesla has not publicly explained the latest pricing decisions. What went wrong with Cybertruck? Unveiled in 2019 and launched in late 2023, Cybertruck was promoted as a futuristic challenger to conventional American pickup trucks. However, the vehicle's unconventional stainless-steel design, high prices, safety recalls and quality-control concerns have complicated its commercial journey. According to Cox Automotive estimates, Tesla sold approximately 20,237 Cybertrucks in the United States in 2025, compared with 38,965 in 2024, a decline of around 48 per cent. Sales remained under pressure in 2026, with an estimated 7,263 Cybertrucks sold during the first six months, down more than 32 per cent from the corresponding period a year earlier. The numbers are significantly below Musk's earlier expectations of eventually producing and selling hundreds of thousands of Cybertrucks annually. Tesla's third-quarter 2026 delivery figures further highlight the challenge. The company delivered just 8,295 vehicles in its 'Other Models' category, which includes Cybertruck, compared with 478,237 Model 3 and Model Y vehicles. While Tesla does not separately disclose Cybertruck deliveries, the figures underline its limited contribution to overall vehicle sales. Why is Musk betting big on Cybercab? Cybercab represents a substantially different business opportunity. Unlike Cybertruck, which is designed for individual ownership, Cybercab is a purpose-built autonomous vehicle intended primarily for robotaxi operations. The two-seater vehicle lacks traditional steering controls and pedals, reflecting Musk's ambition to develop transportation services that operate without human drivers. Tesla began deploying Cybercabs in its Austin robotaxi fleet in September 2026, and its management said in October that it was targeting initial customer deliveries before the end of the year. For Musk, autonomous ride-hailing potentially offers a recurring revenue model in which Tesla can earn money from passenger journeys rather than depending exclusively on vehicle sales. Repurposing Cybertruck manufacturing space could enable Tesla to expand Cybercab output without building an entirely new production facility. However, the robotaxi business faces considerable regulatory and technological challenges. The US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has been examining Cybercab's compliance with federal vehicle safety requirements, particularly because the vehicle lacks conventional manual controls. Commercial success will depend on Tesla's ability to demonstrate safe autonomous driving, secure regulatory compliance and achieve profitable operations at scale. Did the US midterm elections and AI stock rout influence Musk's decision? The announcement comes against an increasingly uncertain political and financial backdrop for Musk's businesses. The November 3 US midterm elections delivered control of both chambers of Congress to Democrats, a setback for President Donald Trump and the Republican Party, which Musk had financially supported. The results have raised concerns among investors about the possibility of greater congressional scrutiny of Musk's businesses, including government contracts, regulatory relationships and artificial intelligence investments. Tesla and SpaceX shares also came under heavy selling pressure this week as the broader US technology sector suffered a sharp correction amid concerns over elevated AI valuations and spending. However, there is no evidence establishing that the election results or stock-market downturn directly triggered the Cybertruck decision. Tesla's shift towards autonomous vehicles and robotics was already underway well before the elections. The developments nevertheless highlight a changing investment environment in which companies pursuing ambitious AI projects face increasing pressure to demonstrate commercially viable returns. Musk's decision is therefore more clearly explained by Cybertruck's disappointing sales performance and Tesla's long-term autonomous mobility strategy than by an immediate reaction to political or financial-market developments. What does this mean for Tesla's future? The proposed Cybertruck wind-down could represent one of Tesla's most significant changes in manufacturing priorities in recent years. It suggests the company is increasingly prepared to redirect resources away from underperforming vehicle programmes towards artificial intelligence, robotics and autonomous transportation. Earlier in 2026, Tesla also announced plans to discontinue production of its Model S and Model X vehicles to free up manufacturing space for its Optimus humanoid robot programme. Together, these decisions underline Musk's ambition to reshape Tesla from a traditional electric vehicle manufacturer into a technology-driven company with multiple revenue streams. For existing Cybertruck owners and prospective buyers, however, uncertainty remains over the vehicle's long-term production, availability, servicing and resale prospects. Tesla has yet to clarify whether the planned wind-down would eventually mean a complete end to Cybertruck manufacturing or merely a substantial reduction in production. The larger question is whether Cybercab can deliver the commercial scale and profitability that Cybertruck has so far failed to achieve. For Musk, the shift represents a major bet on autonomous transportation, even as one of Tesla's most recognisable vehicles moves closer to an uncertain future.
